title: Proverbs 7:1–5
context: A father urges his son to keep his words and commandments as life itself, to guard them like the apple of his eye, bind them on his fingers, and write them on his heart. He is to treat wisdom as a sister and understanding as kin, so that they will protect him from the smooth words of the strange woman.

verses.text: My son, keep my words. Lay up my commandments within you.
verses.arminianNotes: The father’s appeal assumes a son who must choose to keep and treasure instruction. Arminian readers see wisdom offered and received through responsive attention: storing up commands is an active, ongoing habit of the heart.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the covenant household as God’s ordinary means of grace, with parents teaching God’s ways. They read the call to lay up commandments as the duty of a covenant child, fulfilled where God renews the heart.

verses.text: Keep my commandments and live! Guard my teaching as the apple of your eye.
verses.arminianNotes: Keep my commandments and live connects wisdom with life, echoing Deuteronomy’s blessings. The apple of your eye, the pupil, pictures careful protection. Arminian readers stress that the outcome follows the son’s faithful keeping.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that the path of wisdom is the path of life and read live within the covenant setting. Obedience is the way of life God appoints, not the ground of acceptance with him.

verses.text: Bind them on your fingers. Write them on the tablet of your heart.
verses.arminianNotes: Bind them on your fingers and write them on your heart echoes Deuteronomy 6:8 and 11:18. Arminian readers see outward reminders and inward commitment working together in a life of chosen obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers connect the tablet of your heart with the new-covenant promise of Jeremiah 31:33, where God writes his law on the heart. The father’s command anticipates what God’s Spirit accomplishes.

verses.text: Tell wisdom, “You are my sister.” Call understanding your relative,
verses.arminianNotes: Calling wisdom your sister and understanding your relative pictures intimate, familiar companionship. Arminian readers note that wisdom is to be embraced as a chosen relationship, not merely studied.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same imagery of closeness. Wisdom, personified here and in chapter 8, is a loving companion who guards the heart, in contrast to the seductress who follows.

verses.text: that they may keep you from the strange woman, from the foreigner who flatters with her words.
verses.arminianNotes: Wisdom keeps the son from the strange woman, the foreigner who flatters. The terms mark her as outside the covenant bond of marriage, whatever her ethnicity. Arminian readers see wisdom as protection a person can embrace or neglect, with real danger in neglecting it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see wisdom as God’s means of preserving his people from sin. Many also read the strange woman as a figure for folly and false worship more broadly, while keeping the literal warning against adultery central.
